```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

## 1. Background and goal

Accelerometers on the belt, forearm, arm and dumbbell of 6 participants recorded barbell lifts done correctly (class A) and incorrectly in 4 ways (classes B-E). The goal is to predict the `classe` variable from the sensor data and apply the model to 20 test cases. Data come from the Human Activity Recognition project (Velloso, Bulling, Gellersee, Ugulino, Fuks, PUC-Rio): <http://web.archive.org/web/20161224072740/http:/groupware.les.inf.puc-rio.br/har>

## 2. Load data

```{r load}
library(caret)
library(randomForest)

train_url <- "https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/pml-training.csv"
test_url  <- "https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/pml-testing.csv"

training <- read.csv(train_url, na.strings = c("NA", "", "#DIV/0!"))
testing  <- read.csv(test_url,  na.strings = c("NA", "", "#DIV/0!"))
dim(training); dim(testing)
```

## 3. Cleaning and feature selection

I removed (1) identifier/timestamp columns (first 7), which are not sensor measurements, (2) columns that are mostly NA (more than 95% missing; these are summary statistics only filled on window-end rows), and (3) near-zero-variance predictors.

```{r clean}
training <- training[, -(1:7)]
testing  <- testing[,  -(1:7)]

na_share <- colMeans(is.na(training))
keep <- names(na_share[na_share < 0.95])
training <- training[, keep]

nzv <- nearZeroVar(training[, -ncol(training)])
if (length(nzv) > 0) training <- training[, -nzv]

training$classe <- factor(training$classe)

predictors <- setdiff(names(training), "classe")
testing <- testing[, predictors]
length(predictors)
```

## 4. Validation split and cross-validation

I held out 25% of the training data as a validation set to estimate out-of-sample error independently. Within the remaining 75%, I used 5-fold cross-validation for model fitting.

```{r split}
set.seed(2026)
idx <- createDataPartition(training$classe, p = 0.75, list = FALSE)
train_set <- training[idx, ]
valid_set <- training[-idx, ]
```

## 5. Model building

I chose a random forest because it handles many correlated predictors, non-linear relationships and mixed scales without much preprocessing, and typically performs very well on accelerometer data. I also fit a decision tree (rpart) as a simple baseline.

```{r models, cache=TRUE}
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5)

set.seed(2026)
fit_rf <- train(classe ~ ., data = train_set, method = "rf",
                trControl = ctrl, ntree = 100)

set.seed(2026)
fit_tree <- train(classe ~ ., data = train_set, method = "rpart",
                  trControl = ctrl)

fit_rf$results[, c("mtry", "Accuracy", "Kappa")]
max(fit_tree$results$Accuracy)
```

```{r varimp, fig.height=4}
plot(varImp(fit_rf), top = 15, main = "Top 15 predictors (random forest)")
```

## 6. Out-of-sample error

```{r oos}
pred_valid <- predict(fit_rf, valid_set)
cm <- confusionMatrix(pred_valid, valid_set$classe)
cm$table
cm$overall["Accuracy"]
oos_error <- 1 - cm$overall["Accuracy"]
oos_error
```

The cross-validated accuracy on the training folds and the accuracy on the untouched validation set agree closely. The expected out-of-sample error is the validation error above (1 - accuracy), which is well under 1%. Error on new participants could be somewhat higher.

## 7. Predictions for the 20 test cases

```{r predict}
final_pred <- predict(fit_rf, testing)
data.frame(case = 1:20, prediction = final_pred)
```

## 8. Conclusion

A random forest with 5-fold cross-validation, trained on cleaned sensor features, predicts exercise quality with very high accuracy. The predictions above were submitted to the course prediction quiz.

## Citation

Velloso, E.; Bulling, A.; Gellersen, H.; Ugulino, W.; Fuks, H. Qualitative Activity Recognition of Weight Lifting Exercises. Proceedings of 4th International Conference in Cooperation with SIGCHI (Augmented Human '13). Stuttgart, Germany: ACM SIGCHI, 2013.
